main.text: [III, 149] [col. 375] Chapter 3.
It is proved that כפיר chephir and שחל sachal are names not only of lions, as is commonly held, but also of serpents.

The name of the lion is shared by several animals very different from the lion. Thus [col. 376] Diphilus in Athenaeus, Pliny and Aelian describe a λέοντα θαλάττιον [leonta thalattion], a sea lion, among the kinds of lobster. A species of lizard or gecko is ὁ χαμαιλέων [ho chamaileōn], that is, the ground lion; in Arabic the same animal is called ^{a)} ليث عفرين [layth ʿifrīn], the lion of Iphrin, from a place in Arabia where it is common. Similar is the fact that ليث [layth], lion, in Alcamus is ضرب من العناكب [ḍarb min al-ʿanākib], a species of spider. And in the serpent kind the cenchris or cenchrines ^{(1)} is called by some λέων αἴολος [leōn aiolos], the variegated lion. Nicander in the Theriaca, line 463:
Δήεις κεγχρίνου δολιχὸν τέρας, ὅν τε λέοντα Αἴολον αὐδάξαντο, περίστικτον φολίδεσσι· [Dēeis kenchrinou dolichon teras, hon te leonta / Aiolon audaxanto, peristikton pholidessi]

You will find the long monster of the cenchrines, which they have also called the variegated lion, spotted with scales. On these words the Scholiast says: Ἔστι δὲ οὗτος μακρὸς κατάστικτος, ὃν καὶ λέοντά φησι καλεῖν· ἢ διὰ τὸ πολύστικτον τῶν φολίδων· ἢ διὰ δὲ γενναῖον λέοντα ἐκάλουν αὐτόν· ἤτοι διὰ τὸ ὀρθὴν τὴν οὐρὰν βαστάζοντα διεγείρειν ἑαυτὸν εἰς μάχην· ἢ διὰ τὸ δάκνειν, καὶ ῥοφᾷν τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἅτινα δὲ καὶ λέων ποιεῖ [Esti de houtos makros katastiktos, hon kai leonta phēsi kalein; ē dia to polystikton tōn pholidōn; ē dia de gennaion leonta ekaloun auton; ētoi dia to orthēn tēn ouran bastazonta diegeirein heauton eis machēn; ē dia to daknein, kai rhophan to haima tou anthrōpou, hatina de kai leōn poiei]. In these words, why should it be said that it is called lion διὰ τὸ πολύστικτον τῶν φολίδων [dia to polystikton tōn pholidōn], on account of its spotted scales, when there is nothing of the kind in the lion? But the Scholiast had written ὃν καὶ λέοντα αἰολόν φησι καλεῖν [hon kai leonta aiolon phēsi kalein]. His meaning, then, is this: it is called lion because of its noble spirit; or because it rouses itself to fight with its tail erect; or because it bites in the manner of lions and sucks out human blood; but it is called variegated because of the spots sprinkled over its scales. However that may be, it is clear from this that the Greeks too applied the name of lions to serpents, so that no one should find it strange that the Hebrew names of lions, כפיר chephir and שחל sachal, also apply to serpents. Hence, although כפיר chephir properly means young lion, it is nevertheless sometimes taken by the Elders for a dragon. Thus in Iob. IV, 10 they render the Hebrew ושני כפירים נתעו, And the teeth of the chephirim (or young lions) are torn out, with remarkable freedom as γαυρίαμα δὲ δρακόντων ἐσβέσθη [gauriama de drakontōn esbesthē], but the boasting of the dragons is extinguished. And in Iob. XXXVIII, 39., for the Hebrew וחית כפירים תמלא, Will you fill the appetite of the young lions? [III, 150] they have Ψυχὰς δὲ δρακόντων ἐμπλήσεις; [Psychas de drakontōn emplēseis;] Will you satisfy the appetites of the dragons? Evidently כפיר chephir among the Hebrews meant not only young lion but also young dragon ^{(2)}. So too the Arabic شبل [shibl] sabl, which corresponds exactly to the Hebrew כפיר chephir, is generally taken for a young lion. Yet that it is also used of the young of a dragon is shown by these words of the Arabic paraphrast on Thren. IV, 3.: والتنانين خلعوا ثديهم اشبالهم ارضعوا [wa-l-tanānīn khalaʿū thudīyahum ashbālahum arḍaʿū] And the dragons drew out their breasts, they suckled their young. Sea dragons, that is, whales, as is the Hebrew תנין and the Greek δράκοντες [drakontes] in this very passage.

Likewise the word שחל sachal, although elsewhere it means lion, is nevertheless taken by the most ancient translators in Psal. XCI, 13. for the asp or some other serpent. There the Elders render the Hebrew words על שחל ופתן תדרך as Ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδα καὶ βασιλίσκον ἐπιβήσῃ [Ep᾽ aspida kai basiliskon epibēsē]. And the Vulgate translator: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk. And Jerome: You shall tread upon the asp [col. 377] and the basilisk. And Apollinaris:
Ἀσπίδα θαρσαλέως ἐπιβήσῃ, καὶ βασιλίσκον. [Aspida tharsaleōs epibēsē, kai basiliskon.]

And the Syriac: ܥܠ ܓܪܣܐ ܘܥܠ ܚܪܡܢܐ ܬܕܘܫ. And the Arabic: تطا علي الافعي والحية التنين [taṭā ʿalī al-afʿī wa-l-ḥayya al-tinnīn]. And the Ethiopic: ላዕለ፡ ተኵላ፡ ወከይሲ፡ ትጼዐን፡ All in the same sense. For none of them understands a lion here by the word שחל, but some kind of serpent, although they do not agree on the species. For to the Arabic translator שחל is الافعي [al-afʿī], the viper; to the Syriac ܓܪܣܐ, the amphisbaena; to the Ethiopic ተኵላ፡, a kind of serpent so called from its wolf-like nature. And in that whole verse, על שחל ופתן תדרך תרמס כפיר ותנין, it is probable that David dealt only with serpents, and therefore that by the words כפיר and שחל snakes are meant just as much as by the words פתן and תנין, of which the former signifies the asp, the latter the dragon. For thus everything will cohere better than if you mix lions with serpents, as the modern translators do, who here generally have: You shall walk upon the lion and the basilisk, you shall trample the young lion and the dragon. In these words, besides the fact that beasts of entirely different nature are joined together, no one could easily say what it means to walk upon a lion or to tread on a young lion. For there is no one who treads on a lion while walking, as we commonly do on asps and the other kinds of snakes ^{(3)}.

[III, 151] Now, if you ask what kind of snake is signified by the name שחל sachal, I will answer: just as among lions the one called שחל sachal is the one that is black, as we showed in its place ^{b)}, so also a black serpent is designated by the same word. Nicander in the Theriaca describes many of this kind, as when he writes of the asp in verse 172.

Χροιὴ δ᾽ ἄλλοτε μὲν ψαφαροῖς ἐπιδέδρομε νώτοις ῎Αλλοτε μειλινόεσσα, καὶ αἴολος, ἄλλοτε τεφρὴ, Πολλάκι δ᾽ αἰθαλόεσσα, μελαινομένη ὑπὸ βώλῳ Αἰθιόπων, οἵην δὲ πολύστομος εἰς ἅλα Νεῖλος Πλησάμενος κατέχευεν ἄσιν, προὔτυψε δὲ πόντῳ. [Chroiē d᾽ allote men psapharois epidedrome nōtois / allote meilinoessa, kai aiolos, allote tephrē, / pollaki d᾽ aithaloessa, melainomenē hypo bōlō / Aithiopōn, hoiēn de polystomos eis hala Neilos / plēsamenos katecheuen asin, prouptype de pontō.]

The colour on its rough back sometimes appears quince-yellow and mottled, sometimes ash-grey, often also sooty, blackened under the soil of the Ethiopians, like the mud that the Nile, when full, pours into the sea through its many mouths and drives into the deep. And of the haemorrhous in verse 288.
Ἄλλοτε μὲν χροιῇ ψολόεις, ὁτὲ δ᾽ ἔμπαλιν αἰθὸς, [Allote men chroiē psoloeis, hote d᾽ empalin aithos,]
Sometimes it is fiery in colour, sometimes sooty. And of the dipsas in verse 337.
Αἰὲν ὑποζοφόωσα μελαίνεται ἄκροθεν οὐρὴ, [Aien hypozophoōsa melainetai akrothen ourē,]
The tip of the tail is always darkish and blackens. And of the dryinus in verse 420.
Αἰθαλόεις μὲν νῶτα, — — — [Aithaloeis men nōta,]
Sooty indeed on the back. And of the dragon in verse 438.
Φράζεο καὶ χλοάοντα δαεὶς κύανόν τε δράκοντα, [Phrazeo kai chloaonta daeis kyanon te drakonta,]
Describe too, as one who knows, both the green and the black dragon. But hydri or chelydri too are black. Orpheus on stones, on the stone Ostrites:
Ῥεῖά γε μὴν ἀέκοντα μέλας ἠρύκανεν ὕδρος, [Rheia ge mēn aekonta melas ērykanen hydros,]
The black hydrus held him back against his will. Virgil, Georgics book 2:

And rough tufa, and chalk eaten out by black chelydri. — — — — — [III, 152] Aelian too has black asps and black haemorrhoi, Historia book 6, ch. 38 and book 15, ch. 13. Aëtius describes the ammodytes, marked with black spots; the chelidonian asp, black on the back like swallows and white on the belly; the dipsas with a black tail; and dragons, some black, some red, some ash-grey. Pausanias in the Boeotica says: Ἐν Αἰθιοπίᾳ μέλανας τὰς ἀσπίδας οὐ μεῖον ἢ καὶ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἡ γῆ τρέφει [En Aithiopia melanas tas aspidas ou meion ē kai tous anthrōpous hē gē trephei]; In Ethiopia the earth nourishes black asps no less than black men. In Avicenna the swallow serpent, that is, the chelidonian asp, [col. 378] لونها يشبه لون الخطاف [lawnuhā yushbihu lawn al-khaṭṭāf] is in colour like a swallow, that is, with a black back. And the colour of the basilisk inclines الي سواد وصفرة [ilā sawād wa-ṣufra] to blackness and yellowness. The haemorrhous too and the cerastes (in the barbarous writers aufudius and sabrin) have نقط سود وبيض [nuqaṭ sūd wa-bīḍ] black and white spots sprinkled over their body; and heads and tails sometimes سودا وحمرا وبيضا [sūdan wa-ḥumran wa-bīḍan] black, red and white. On the body of the dipsas, too, there are اثار سود كثيرة [āthār sūd kathīra] very many traces of blackness: ولون موخرها الي الاذناب الي السواد [wa-lawn muʾakhkharihā ilā al-adhnāb ilā al-sawād] and the colour of the hind part towards the tail inclines to blackness. And the same author says of dragons: ولها وجوه صفرا وسودا [wa-lahā wujūh ṣufran wa-sūdan] They have yellow and black faces. Nor do the more recent writers say otherwise. For Belon, an eyewitness (αὐτόπτης [autoptēs]), in the Observations book 1, ch. 31 and book 2, ch. 14, describes the jaculus as sprinkled with black spots like eyes. And Gesner describes the typhlops as dusky over the whole body, or darkly spotted. And Olaus Magnus, in his description of the Northern lands, says that serpents of black colour inhabit partly the waters, partly the land; and that serpents dwelling among rocks are mostly black, which in the vernacular of the people they call Snok. I understand snakes, which are called Snake in English. Rightly, then, does the greatest poet say in book 1 of the Georgics:
He added baneful poison to black serpents:

that is, many of which are black in colour. Yet one serpent is black above the rest, and for that very reason it is called in Arabic اسود [aswad] asuad, that is, black. Alcamus: الاسود الحية العظيمة [al-aswad al-ḥayya al-ʿaẓīma] Alasuad (the black one), a great serpent ^{(4)}. Some add سالخ [sālikh] salich as an epithet, as if you were to say one coming out [III, 153], which Damir explains thus: الاسود السالخ نوع من الحيات شديد السواد سمي بذلك لانه يسلخ جلده كل عام [al-aswad al-sālikh nawʿ min al-ḥayyāt shadīd al-sawād summiya bi-dhālika li-annahu yaslukhu jildahu kull ʿām] Alasuad assalich, a kind of serpent of the most intense blackness, which is so called because it sheds its skin every year. Another copy has نوع من الافعوان [nawʿ min al-afʿuwān] a kind of viper. I understand black asps, which many Arabs include under the kind of vipers. These asps are indeed very black, as besides Nicander is taught by Pausanias, Aelian, Aëtius, and some of the Arabs. Granted this, the ancients rightly interpret שחל sachal as asp. Damir tells many fables about the black serpent, which I am loath to relate here. Among them: that Jesus, son of Mary, foretold to a woodcutter that on that very day he would fall into the gravest danger to his life. When he had gone to cut wood and returned towards evening with a bundle of wood, and at Christ's command had untied it, he found in it حية سودا [ḥayya sūdā] a black serpent. Then, when Jesus asked what he had done, and he denied having done anything except that he had given part of his bread to a passing beggar, Jesus replied: بهذا دفع عنك [bi-hādhā dafaʿa ʿanka] For this reason God has turned evil away from you. Others tell the same of [col. 379] Saleh, the prophet, and say that the serpent اسود سالخ [aswad sālikh] asuad salich was as thick مثل الجذع [mithl al-jidhʿ] as the trunk of a palm.

notes.text: Coluber miliaris, white below, dusky above, with scales marked by a white spot, Linn. See Syst. Nat. T. 1, vol. 3, p. 1099. Cf. Gesner, de Serpentibus fol. 37.

But nothing can be weaker than this opinion of Bochart, since it rests solely on the authority of the Alexandrian translator. And from the fact that the poet Nicander calls the coluber miliaris λέοντα αἰόλον [leonta aiolon], it cannot even be concluded that the Greeks applied the name of lions to serpents, much less the Hebrews.

But since, as we have seen, the name כפיר is taken for a serpent without reason, and [III, 151] means nothing but a lion, it follows that שחל, which in this passage corresponds to כפיר, cannot, by the laws of the parallelism of members, be taken in any other sense than the usual meaning lion. Nor am I moved by Bochart's objection to the common interpretation, that it yields a sense that is not apt enough. For understand lions lying down, which no one strikes with his foot with impunity, just as no one treads on serpents unpunished, and there will be nothing incongruous in this image of the Hebrew poet.

This seems to be the same species of serpent that Forsskål describes in Descript. Animall. p. 15, no. 13. I shall add his words: Coluber, Arab. Hannasch aesvaed, حنش اسود [ḥanash aswad] [black viper]. Entirely black; a cubit long; as thick as a finger; oviparous.
